content: The studies reviewed included both retrospective cohort studies and cost-effectiveness analyses, focusing on the use of antenatal corticosteroids (ACS) for women at risk of preterm birth. Most studies evaluated costs and outcomes over a short time horizon, typically until neonatal hospital discharge. The methodological quality of the studies varied, with four rated as high quality, three as moderate, and one as low. Key Findings on Cost-Effectiveness: 1. General Findings: Five studies concluded that antenatal corticosteroids were both cost-saving and more effective than no treatment. Three studies found that while ACS therapy might increase costs, it was still likely to be cost-effective. 2. Country-Specific Studies: A Canadian study (2000) demonstrated that ACS reduced respiratory distress syndrome (RDS) and neonatal deaths while being less costly than no intervention. A UK study (1991) found ACS to be cost-saving for women up to 31 weeks of gestation, reducing RDS and neonatal deaths. Although total costs increased due to the care of surviving infants, the average cost per survivor was lower compared to no ACS therapy. A U.S. single-center study (1986) showed that ACS reduced hospital charges and provided morbidity benefits for preterm newborns, making it cost-saving. Another U.S. study (1995) reported that ACS reduced hospital costs, deaths, and index cases in infants born weighing less than 2 kg, as well as in preterm infants at 28–31 weeks. For infants born before 28 weeks, fewer deaths were observed, but there were more index cases. Despite this, ACS remained cost-saving in terms of hospital costs. A Netherlands study (1992) found that ACS reduced RDS incidence but increased total hospitalization time and costs due to higher neonatal survival rates. Nevertheless, ACS was considered cost-effective. 3. Global Analysis: A cost-effectiveness analysis of a placebo-controlled trial of dexamethasone in Bangladesh, India, Kenya, Nigeria, and Pakistan (unpublished WHO data) showed that ACS averted 38 neonatal deaths per 1,000 woman-baby units. The intervention was cost-saving in all countries, with savings ranging from $54 per unit in Kenya to $2 per unit in Nigeria. Preterm Birth Studies: Four studies in Ethiopia, South Africa, and the U.S. examined the cost-effectiveness of ACS for preterm births, though gestational age ranges were not always specified. Two studies used the Lives Saved Tool (LiST) for analysis, one used a retrospective cohort study, and another employed decision modeling. Methodological quality was high in two studies and moderate in two. Late Preterm Birth Studies (34 to <37 weeks): Three U.S. studies evaluated the cost-effectiveness of ACS in late preterm births. One study (2012) used a decision model and found that a full course of ACS was cost-effective at 34, 35, and 36 weeks, but a partial course was not. A 2019 study concluded that betamethasone reduced total mean costs for each woman-infant pair compared to placebo. However, a 2020 study, using the same data, reported that betamethasone was not cost-effective in the short term due to additional costs associated with neonatal hypoglycemia and fewer quality-adjusted life years (QALYs) compared to placebo. Feasibility and Acceptability: ACS therapy is relatively inexpensive, easy to administer, and widely available in most settings. It can be integrated into existing health systems with minimal cost. However, successful implementation requires skilled health personnel to identify women at risk of preterm birth, administer intramuscular injections, and monitor care. Accurate gestational age estimation using obstetric ultrasound is also essential. Barriers to implementation include insufficient provider knowledge, outdated guidelines, and logistical challenges such as maintaining consistent stock and identifying preterm labor. Time constraints and high workloads in maternity wards further complicate administration. Equity Considerations: Preterm birth rates and associated neonatal morbidity and mortality are higher in lowand middle-income countries due to limited access to quality healthcare. Women and newborns in disadvantaged settings, such as rural areas or among the poorest populations, are disproportionately affected. Ensuring equitable access to ACS therapy requires addressing these disparities. Additional Considerations: ACS should only be administered in settings where adequate maternal and neonatal care is available. This includes facilities capable of managing preterm newborns and addressing potential side effects of the therapy. Injectable dexamethasone is included in the WHO Essential Medicines List, but betamethasone preparations are not. Ensuring the quality of corticosteroid preparations is critical, as substandard products have been reported in some settings. Conclusion: Antenatal corticosteroids are a cost-effective intervention for reducing neonatal morbidity and mortality associated with preterm birth. However, their implementation requires adequate healthcare infrastructure, trained personnel, and consistent supply chains. Addressing barriers to access and ensuring equitable distribution are essential for maximizing the benefits of this intervention.
